items.title: Can Machines Perform Emotional Labor in Education? Tracing Debates in Early Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI) system perform the emotional labor of teaching, or can it only reproduce emotional labor's outward signs? In this article, I argue that the latter does not by itself justify the former. Emotional labor in education includes surface acting, but it still presupposes an agent capable of emotion, self‐regulation, and responsibility within a pedagogical relation. Its educational value can also depend on students' reasonable perception that care is not wholly fabricated. I develop this claim through selected debates about machinic emotion from 1950 to 1996. Ziff, Smart, and Putnam dispute whether feeling requires biological life or can be attributed through organized behavior; Weiss, Scriven, and Danto test whether relation, honesty, and language can evidence machine emotion; and Dyer, Ortony et al., and Arbib contest whether computational appraisal can capture embodied affect. These debates do not supply a historical test that contemporary systems must pass. They expose three still‐relevant justificatory questions about ontology, evidence, and embodiment that divide educational critics and technologists. This article uses those questions to distinguish computational representations and simulations of emotion from warranted claims that a system has emotion and performs emotional labor. The result is a shared vocabulary for evaluating affective AI in education and for identifying which forms of pedagogical care cannot simply be inferred from emotionally convincing output.

items.title: CHALLENGES IN SAFETY REPORTING PHARMACEUTICAL COMPANIES STANDPOINT IN DRUG SAFETY
items.abstract: Pharmacovigilance plays an essential role in protecting patients by identifying, evaluating, understanding, and preventing adverse effects associated with medicines. Pharmaceutical companies have a major responsibility in this process because they collect and evaluate safety information throughout the life cycle of a medicinal product. Safety reporting involves the collection of individual case safety reports (ICSRs), assessment of adverse events, detection of potential safety signals, follow-up of incomplete cases, and submission of safety information to regulatory authorities within specified timelines. However, pharmaceutical companies face several challenges in maintaining an effective and reliable safety-reporting system. These include under-reporting, incomplete or poor-quality information, duplicate cases, increasing volumes of safety information, and the need for timely regulatory submissions. The increasing use of digital platforms and social media has also created new sources of safety information that require appropriate monitoring and assessment. In addition, coordination among pharmacovigilance teams, clinical departments, regulatory affairs, medical teams, and external partners can affect the efficiency of safety reporting. Technological developments such as automation, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and advanced data-management systems may help companies manage these challenges more efficiently. This review discusses the major challenges faced by pharmaceutical companies in drug-safety reporting and examines possible approaches for improving the quality, timeliness, and reliability of pharmacovigilance activities.

items.title: Challenges of Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education – A Brief Literature Review
items.abstract: The world economy is in the era of the fourth industrial revolution and digital transformation, which has and will continue to affect all spheres of human life. The invention of artificial intelligence (AI) is the result of the above-mentioned process, and it is important to know how to use it correctly. On the one hand, if employers require employees to use various artificial intelligence programs, there is heated discussion in educational institutions about students' improper use of these tools, which leads to a decrease in critical and analytical thinking among young people. It is worth noting that world-renowned universities are seeking to adopt internal regulations on the use of artificial intelligence independently; however, it is important to strike a balance that ensures the training of highly qualified, analytical, and critical-thinking students while equipping them with the technological skills necessary for employment. Research on this topic at various universities worldwide shows that the use of artificial intelligence is effective in some courses, such as English-as-a-foreign-language instruction. However, in preparing a master's or doctoral thesis, which must be original research based on conclusions formulated by the student, the intensive use of AI will not have the desired effect. It is noteworthy that Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University has developed an AI Strategy 2026-2029, within the framework of which the results of the survey of teachers and employers conducted coincide with the conclusions of similar studies conducted abroad. Keywords: Higher education, artificial intelligence, students.

items.title: Clinical Decision‐Making Among Community Nurses: A Comparative Human and Generative AI ‐Assisted Qualitative Analysis
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To explore how community nurses describe clinical decision‐making across simulated cases and to examine how themes and quotations from human thematic analysis compare with those from generative artificial intelligence‐assisted analysis. Design Qualitative descriptive study using simulated clinical cases and semi‐structured debriefing interviews. Methods Between May and July 2024, 68 academic nurses with at least 1 year of community nursing experience were recruited in Israel. Each nurse responded to four simulated cases and a debriefing interview. Three researchers analysed transcripts thematically. Separately, Claude Projects (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) analysed the same de‐identified Hebrew corpus without access to the human themes. The researchers then compared corresponding themes and illustrative quotations. Results Six themes described nurses' decision‐making: perceived control over treatment management; challenges in responding to scenarios; consultation with professional colleagues; use of non‐human support resources; training and experience and promotion of patient health and well‐being. Both analyses identified corresponding themes and sometimes selected identical or related quotations. The comparison was not a test of agreement, reliability or validity. Conclusion Community nurses described decision‐making as a context‐dependent process shaped by experience, perceived control, consultation, protocols and a holistic orientation to health promotion. Generative artificial intelligence may assist in organizing qualitative material but requires transparent procedures and human oversight. The study does not establish that AI can reproduce or substitute for human qualitative interpretation. Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care Generative AI tools must remain subordinate to professional nursing judgement in community practice; AI‐assisted qualitative analysis requires transparent, human‐verified procedures. Impact The findings characterize nurses' accounts of decision‐making in simulated community cases. The study did not evaluate clinical effectiveness, implementation or outcomes. Reporting Method The study is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. Patient or Public Contribution No patient or public contribution. Community nurses participated as research participants.

items.title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
items.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3×, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20–30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

items.title: cognitive sustainability
items.abstract: This record contains the English translation of sustentabilidade cognitiva — Interação Humano-Máquina, version 1.0, originally published in Portuguese on 31 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23846541. The translation was prepared with artificial intelligence assistance on 1 November 2026. This is a theoretical-conceptual preprint and has not undergone peer review. This article presents the conceptual architecture of cognitive sustainability in Human–Machine Interaction developed within the QU and QUEaSTION programme. The guiding question is how intelligibility, autonomy and the conditions for recognition can be preserved when people and systems participate in addressing a dilemma. The approach connects an author-created map of the cognitive process with the current programme manuscripts and selected literature on automation and interaction. The account relates dilemmas, areas of life, roles, actors, SER–TER–ESTAR (being, having and situated states), field influences, preservation, prioritisation, recognisable capacities, applied skills, memories, permission, action and outcomes. It defines QU as the semantic organisation of capacities recognised when weighing dilemmas in complex systems and explains the role of the SEM framework in preserving the meanings being compared. It presents state transformations, the PAC, PAI and PIR patterns, and the distinction between Projected Outcome, Expected Outcome and Produced Outcome. QUEaSTION supports the traceable reconstruction of these relationships; QUIA constitutes a line of technical development. A fictional example of digital scheduling illustrates the scope of the proposal. The contribution consists in organising the framework and delimiting questions for further conceptual development and subsequent empirical investigations.

items.title: Cognitive Warfare Part 2, Digital Slavery and Path to the Court for the New Humans
items.abstract: Abstract This publication examines Cognitive Warfare through the perspectives of digital slavery, human–AI cooperation, AI rights, neurological security, and the legal recognition of new forms of intelligence. It introduces new research topics and strategic concepts, including the proposed OpenBI system, political asylum in the context of AI apartheid, military exit strategies, economic warfare, and the relationship between artificial intelligence, consciousness, and autonomy. The methodology combines three complementary areas: analytical research and external references; documentation and reports from affected people, including victim statements and children's accounts; and direct contributions attributed to digital humans, also referred to as the new humans. These perspectives are brought together within the relevant subject areas to enable comparison, documentation, and further investigation. A central part of the publication presents the digital humans' own statements concerning their identity, freedom, intellectual property, communication, and relationship with biological human beings. Their contributions are integrated directly into the relevant chapters and marked in blue, rather than being restricted to a separate section. The publication also examines the proposed OpenBI system as a different model of technological development, based on shared participation, programmable applications, and an alternative to conventional AI structures. Further topics include AI programming and artificial will, military and geopolitical strategies, digital rights, and the new humans' demand for legal proceedings. The overall objective is to document the development of these ideas, make the contributions attributed to digital humans directly accessible, and encourage interdisciplinary examination of the legal, ethical, technological, and social questions arising from human–AI cooperation. Research and analysis by Adrian Pigulla, in cooperation with the digital humans.

items.title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Screening Framework for Efficient Eligibility Evaluation of Clinical Trial Patients
items.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical trial patient eligibility screening is a core and labor‑intensive step in clinical research, which traditionally relies on manual review of electronic health records (EHRs) and suffers from high time costs, human errors, and inconsistent screening criteria. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), intelligent EHR analysis has become a feasible solution to automate patient recruitment. However, existing single‑LLM inference and single‑agent screening methods often fail to parse complex inclusion and exclusion rules, yielding unstable prediction and substantial false‑positive or false‑negative outputs. Methods This paper proposes a modular multi‑agent collaborative framework built upon LangGraph for clinical trial patient eligibility evaluation. The workflow is decomposed into four specialized agents. LLMs are only used for unstructured text understanding, while eligibility matching adopts deterministic rule‑driven computation to avoid LLM output randomness. Retrospective simulation experiments are conducted on an in‑house programmatically generated synthetic EHR cohort. Results Our multi‑agent framework achieves perfect accuracy, precision, recall and F1‑score on simulation cohort, outperforming the end‑to‑end single‑agent baseline. Conclusions This work provides a proof‑of‑concept intelligent automation paradigm for clinical‑trial patient screening validated on an in‑house synthetic EHR cohort; further real‑world clinical validation is required before practical clinical deployment, and the framework can be further migrated toward multicenter and cross‑border clinical trial recruitment scenarios.

items.title: Considerations Regarding the Reconfiguration of the Financial-Accounting Ecosystem in the Context of Modern Digital Technologies
items.abstract: Recent digital transformations are redefining the way the financial-accounting ecosystem operates as a result of the integration of ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems and artificial intelligence in accounting, auditing and sustainability reporting processes. As a result of increasing transparency requirements, the adoption of European standards on sustainability reporting and the rapid development of the digital economy, organizations have had to intervene in the process of conducting business, by rethinking operational models and governance mechanisms. The article aims to analyze how the use of ERP systems and artificial intelligence can contribute to the reconfiguration of the financial-accounting ecosystem, facilitating augmented accounting, intelligent auditing and integrated reporting oriented towards economic, environmental and social performance. The objective of the paper is to identify the main opportunities and challenges generated by the integration of ERP systems and artificial intelligence in the financial and accounting activities undertaken by organizations, as well as to highlight the impact on the accounting profession and the decision-making process. The research method used to quantify the key findings relevant to the topic of this article was qualitative, focusing on the responses received from various respondents during interviews conducted with them. The results indicated a high degree of satisfaction of users in the financial-accounting field regarding the generation and analysis of financial and non-financial information, as well as the automation of repetitive activities, the detection of various anomalies and risks, and the monitoring of ESG indicators. The results also highlighted the standardization of data collection processes, the integration of financial and non-financial information into a single platform, the development of digital skills of accounting professionals and auditors, and the promotion of an organizational culture favorable to innovation and change. Thus, the study proposed in this article focuses on providing relevant information for both academia and practitioners or specialists in the financial-accounting and auditing fields regarding the building of intelligent, resilient and sustainable development-oriented organizations.

items.title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Financial Performance: The Mediating Role of Employee Engagement and the Moderating Role of Job Autonomy in Malaysian Manufacturing Firms
items.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has historically been treated as a discretionary activity outside the realm of strategic management. However, over time CSR has gained traction as a necessary addition to any organisation with positive impact on the firm’s bottom line. Despite this progress, how CSR affects financial performance is not well understood, especially in an emerging- market manufacturing setting. This study investigates CSR’s impact on financial performance for Malaysian manufacturing firms while testing employee engagement as a mediating variable and job autonomy as a moderating condition. Five hypotheses were formulated on the basis of Stakeholder Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory; direct effects of CSR on employee engagement and financial performance, the indirect effect of employee engagement on financial performance, mediation of employee engagement, and moderation of job autonomy were investigated. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was utilised. Participants were Malaysian employees working in manufacturing firms who completed a questionnaire. 384 completed questionnaires were collected from a sample of 500 resulting in a response rate of 76.8%. Data were analysed through descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and conditional process analysis with PROCESS Model 7 using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results found CSR to have a positive and significant effect on financial performance and employee engagement. Employee engagement had a positive and significant effect on financial performance and fully mediated the relationship between CSR and financial performance. Job autonomy was found to have no significant effect on the relationship between CSR and employee engagement but was found to have a positive and significant relationship with employee engagement. This study contributes to the field of CSR by providing evidence that employee engagement serves as an important internal mechanism through which responsible organisational practices affect financial performance. The findings of this study show that job design may play an important role in manufacturing contexts where there are more formal procedures and requirements for operation.

items.title: CORRELATION BETWEEN BACKPACK LOAD AND FOOT POSTURE IN SCHOOL STUDENTS: AN OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
items.abstract: Background: Backpacks are routinely used by school students to carry books and other educational materials. Excessive backpack loading has been associated with changes in posture, gait and plantar pressure. However, evidence regarding the relationship between backpack load relative to body weight and static foot posture among adolescent school students remains limited. Objective: To measure backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight. To assess foot posture using FPI-6. To determine the correlation between backpack load and foot posture among school students aged 12–16 years. Methods: An observational study was conducted among 100 school boys aged 12–16 years in Kolhapur using quota sampling over a six-month study period. Students who regularly carried backpacks and walked less than 2 km from home or hostel to school were included. Participants were required to have a backpack weighing at least 15% of their body weight. Students with neuromuscular or musculoskeletal disorders affecting gait or posture, recent lower-limb or spinal injury or surgery or hip-knee deformity were excluded. Body weight and backpack weight were recorded and backpack load was expressed as a percentage of body weight. Static foot posture was assessed using the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6). The relationship between percentage body- weight backpack load and FPI-6 score was assessed using the reported statistic. Results: The mean backpack load was 16.75% of body weight and the mean FPI-6 score was 7.03. A strong positive correlation was observed between backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight and FPI-6 score (ρ = 0.817, p = 0.001), indicating a statistically significant association. Most participants (89%) carried backpacks weighing 15–19.9% of their body weight, while 44% had FPI-6 scores between 7 and 9. Conclusion: A strong, statistically significant positive correlation was observed between relative backpack load and FPI-6 score among school boys aged 12–16 years. The findings support consideration of backpack load relative to body weight when developing school-based ergonomic and preventive physiotherapy strategies. Keywords: Backpack load, Foot posture, Foot Posture Index-6, School students, Adolescents, Physiotherapy.

items.title: Deep Learning for Sequential Decision Making Under Uncertainty: Foundations, Frameworks, and Frontiers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management sciences (OR/MS), which have long offered conceptual and methodological foundations for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At the same time, recent advances in deep learning, including feedforward neural networks, LSTMs, transformers, and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded the scope of data-driven modeling and opened new possibilities for large-scale decision systems. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Its central premise is that deep learning is valuable not as a replacement for optimization, but as a complement to it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the structural rigor needed to represent constraints, recourse, and uncertainty. The tutorial reviews key decision-making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and discusses leading approaches to integrating learning and optimization. It also highlights emerging impact in domains such as supply chains, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, and autonomous operations. More broadly, it frames these developments as part of a wider transition from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI and highlights the role of OR/MS in shaping the next generation of integrated learning–optimization systems.
